newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Trade pact will make infotechnology goods cheaper.
newsitem.headline: Trade pact will make infotechnology goods cheaper.

text.p: Cars, telephones, sewing machines and computer software are among the vast range of goods that should become cheaper thanks to a sweeping deal clinched on Thursday to scrap import taxes on information technology.

"Almost every family is using equipment in the field of information technology. Prices will come down because of the agreement we've just achieved," Dutch trade minister Anneke van Dok told reporters.
Trade in information technology (IT) already approaches $600 billion a year and was set to double by the end of the century even before Thursday's agreement.
The pact, covering 300 product categories, is likely to be the crowning achievement of this week's inaugural ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Singapore.

About 30 countries are due to sign the pact on Friday and many more by mid-March -- the deadline set by the United States and the European Union (EU) to sign up countries accounting for 90 percent of world trade in IT.

"It will be good for the IT industry, and will act as a catalyst for industrial growth. As such it will be good for the whole world economy," Sir Leon Brittan, the EU commissioner for trade, said in a statement.

The agreement was clinched after months of horse trading and intensive lobbying by industries and individual firms, which helps explain some apparently curious omissions in the list of products on which tariffs are to be scrapped by 2000.
Digital photocopiers, for example, which make up the bulk of new copiers on the market, are included. But older, non-digital ones are not.
Fibre-optic cables, which are replacing copper wires in telephone transmission, are included. But the optic fibres that are needed for the manufacturing of such cables are not.
Computer screens are included, but the graphic display tubes they use are not.

And to exclude domestic television sets from the agreement, comupter screens are defined as having a "dot screen pitch" of less than 0.4 millimetre. The dots on TV screens are more widely spaced, because they are viewed from farther away, and so will remain subject to import tariffs.
The purpose of the pact was to scrap tariffs on industrial -- not consumer -- IT equipment and related goods.
But everyday consumer items such as telephones, pagers and fax machines are embraced in the catch-all category of telecommunications equipment.
Another important product is capacitors -- energy-saving devices that are used in computers and a host of electronic products such as tape recorders.
Semiconductors, the ubiquitous chips that are the heart of not only computers but most household electronic goods, cameras and car electronics, are also in the IT agreement.
Audio and film recordings are excluded in deference to those countries such as France that are anxious to protect their home-grown cultural output from a flood of foreign films and music.
But all computer software, including CD-ROM data storage discs, are covered by the agreement.
